guide.title: Cardiac Arrest & High-Quality CPR
guide.lead: Survival comes from compressions and early shocks. Push hard and fast, let the chest come all the way up, and never stop for long. Watch the capnograph: it tells you how good your CPR is and when the heart comes back.

sections.title: High-quality CPR: the numbers
rows: At least 5 cm (2 inches), not more than 6 cm (2.4 inches)
At least 60%, aim for 80% or more
1 breath every 6 seconds (10 breaths/min), compressions continuous

sections.title: Shock or no shock

steps.text: Shock, then CPR for 2 minutes straight away.
Epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO every 3–5 minutes after the first shocks fail.
Amiodarone 300 mg, then 150 mg (or lidocaine 1–1.5 mg/kg, then 0.5–0.75 mg/kg).
CPR for 2 minutes between rhythm checks.
Epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO as soon as possible, then every 3–5 minutes.
Find and treat the cause (Hs and Ts).

sections.after: Advanced airway and drugs never at the cost of compressions.

sections.title: Read the capnograph
rows: Poor compressions, or a very poor outlook if it stays low
Switch compressor; check depth, rate, recoil
Sudden jump to 35–45 mmHg or more
Check for a pulse at the next pause

quiz.q: EtCO₂ stays at 8 mmHg after 6 minutes of CPR and the compressor is tiring. Best action?
options: Switch compressors and check depth, rate and recoil
Keep the same compressor to avoid a pause

quiz.q: Ventilation rate with an advanced airway in place during CPR:
At a rhythm check, EtCO₂ jumps from 12 to 52 mmHg. Most likely?
quiz.explanation: A sudden rise is the earliest sign of ROSC.
Faster than 120 reduces depth and filling.

options: At least 5 cm, not more than 6 cm

quiz.q: Compression-to-ventilation ratio for an adult without an advanced airway:
quiz.explanation: With an advanced airway: continuous compressions.

quiz.q: Maximum time for a pulse check:
An unresponsive patient is gasping occasionally. You should:
options: Treat as cardiac arrest: start CPR
Put them in the recovery position
quiz.explanation: Agonal gasps are not normal breathing.

quiz.q: Epinephrine dose in adult cardiac arrest:
quiz.explanation: As soon as possible for non-shockable rhythms.

quiz.q: First amiodarone dose for shock-refractory VF:

flashcards.question: Chain of survival
flashcards.answer: Early recognition and call for help, early CPR, rapid defibrillation, advanced resuscitation, post-cardiac arrest care, recovery.

flashcards.question: Adult compression rate and depth
flashcards.answer: 100–120/min; at least 5 cm (2 inches), not more than 6 cm (2.4 inches).

flashcards.question: Chest compression fraction
flashcards.answer: The share of arrest time spent compressing: at least 60%, aim for 80% or more.

flashcards.question: Compressions to ventilations
flashcards.answer: 30:2. With an advanced airway: 1 breath every 6 seconds (10 breaths/min) with continuous compressions.

flashcards.question: When to switch compressors
flashcards.answer: Every 2 minutes, or sooner if tiring.

flashcards.question: EtCO₂ below 10 mmHg during CPR
flashcards.answer: Compressions are probably poor: switch compressors and check depth, rate and recoil.

flashcards.question: Earliest sign of ROSC
flashcards.answer: A sudden, sustained rise in EtCO₂ (to 35–45 mmHg or more). Check for a pulse.

flashcards.question: Why full recoil matters
flashcards.answer: The heart refills between compressions; leaning cuts venous return and coronary perfusion.

critical.scenario: A 60-year-old collapsed on a treadmill. Bystander CPR and one AED shock before you arrive. With your team compressing, EtCO₂ is 14 mmHg after 1 minute.
critical.question: What do you prioritise, and what does 14 mmHg mean?

options.t: Keep high-quality 30:2 CPR with minimal pauses, analyse at the end of the cycle; coach depth and rate to push EtCO₂ higher

options.f: Airways never at the cost of compressions.
Above 10 is acceptable, but higher is better.

critical.explanation: Above 10 mmHg shows blood is moving; coaching often raises it further.

critical.scenario: Two-rescuer CPR, fine VF. EtCO₂ 8 mmHg after 4 minutes. Your partner is tiring: shallow compressions about 4 cm, rate about 90/min, leaning between compressions.
critical.question: Most important immediate action?

options.t: Swap compressors now and target 5–6 cm, 100–120/min and full recoil; shock at the next check
Ventilate faster to make up for it
Stop and check for a pulse
options.f: VF has no pulse; keep compressing.

critical.explanation: Fatigue is a common cause of poor CPR. EtCO₂ below 10 mmHg confirms it.

critical.scenario: After one shock and 2 doses of epinephrine, the rhythm check shows narrow complexes at 80/min. EtCO₂ has jumped from 11 to 48 mmHg and there's a strong carotid pulse.
critical.question: What phase is this, and your priorities?

options.t: ROSC: stop compressions, ventilate 10 breaths/min, SpO₂ 92–98%, BP, 12-lead, transport to a PCI-capable cardiac arrest centre
PEA: continue CPR and give more epinephrine

options.f: Re-arrest is common; keep them on.

options.t: Ventilate fast to wash out CO₂

critical.explanation: Post-ROSC care (4.9): avoid hypoxia, hyperoxia, hypotension and hyperventilation; temperature control in hospital.
critical.kpi: ROSC recognition and post-arrest care transition
